title: "Jensen-Shannon Divergence"
description: "A symmetric, finite measure of how different two probability distributions are."
term: "Jensen-Shannon Divergence"
letter: "J"
category: "Statistics"
difficulty: "Advanced"

## Simple explanation

Jensen-Shannon divergence measures how different two probability distributions
are. It compares each distribution with their average, producing a symmetric
score that stays finite even when one distribution assigns zero probability to
an event.

## Technical explanation

For distributions $P$ and $Q$, let $M=(P+Q)/2$. The Jensen-Shannon divergence
is

$$
\operatorname{JSD}(P\|Q)
= \frac{1}{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|M)
+ \frac{1}{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|M),
$$

where $D_{\mathrm{KL}}$ is Kullback-Leibler divergence. With logarithm base 2,
the divergence lies between 0 and 1; with natural logarithms, it lies between
0 and $\ln 2$.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Jensen-Shannon divergence can compare generated and reference distributions,
measure disagreement between models, and define objectives in generative
modeling. Its symmetry and boundedness can make it more convenient than
Kullback-Leibler divergence for certain comparisons.

## How it works

The method first forms the mixture distribution $M$, then measures the
Kullback-Leibler divergence from each input distribution to that mixture. It
averages the two results. Because the mixture includes probability mass from
both distributions, it avoids the infinite divergence that can occur when one
distribution has zero probability where the other does not.

## Practical example

Suppose two language models assign different probabilities to the next-token
choices. Treat each model's normalized scores as a distribution, compute their
mixture, and use the Jensen-Shannon divergence to quantify how much their
predictions differ.

## Common misconceptions

- Jensen-Shannon divergence is symmetric, while Kullback-Leibler divergence
  generally is not.
- The numerical range depends on the logarithm base.
- The square root of Jensen-Shannon divergence is a metric; the divergence
  itself is not usually referred to as a metric.
